name: Dip bars
lead: Dip bars, also called parallel bars or dip stations, are a pair of horizontal handles set at about hip height or higher. The user supports their body on straight arms, lowers until the arms bend to roughly 90 degrees, and presses back up.[1][2] They are sold as freestanding stands, wall-mounted bars, power-rack attachments and small portable units.

The dip is a compound bodyweight pressing exercise that builds the triceps, chest (pectoralis major) and front shoulders (anterior deltoid), the muscles that give the arms, chest and shoulders their size and shape.[1][2] An upright torso and close grip emphasize the triceps, while a forward lean and wider grip shift work toward the chest and shoulders.[1][2] In looksmaxxing and fitness communities dip bars are used to add lower-chest, shoulder and triceps mass at home with bodyweight, and weight can be added with a belt, vest or backpack as the exercise gets easier.[1][2]

No trial has tested dip bars as a product, but general resistance-training meta-analyses show muscle growth across a wide range of loads taken near failure, which is the research basis proponents rely on.[3]

angle.text: Dips are a progressive pressing movement that can be done with only bodyweight. Lifters use them to add size to the triceps, lower chest and shoulders.

paras: In a standard dip the lifter supports the body on straight arms with shoulders over the hands, lowers under control and pushes back up to lockout.[2] Technique guidance advises keeping the shoulders retracted and depressed and controlling the descent to limit excessive shoulder extension.[1] Dips can be made easier with bands, assisted machines or bench dips, and harder with a dip belt, weighted vest or a backpack of weights. A variation uses gymnastic rings, whose instability adds challenge.[2]

Stations range from basic two-post stands to heavy-duty rack-integrated bars. Stability, handle width and handle height most affect how well a station suits the exercise; gymnastics and kettlebell forums discuss parallel bars with a focus on rigidity and adjustable width.[4][5] One T Nation member listing a home setup said a rack with a dip attachment, bench, bar, platform and plates cost under $2,000 in 2017, and called the brand's adjustable bench flimsy.[6]

According to one machine-written encyclopedia entry, the parallel bars were developed by the German educator Friedrich Ludwig Jahn in the 1810s as part of the Turnen gymnastics system, and dip-type exercises later featured in European and US military physical training.[1] The same source says the exercise became a staple of bodybuilding in the 1950s and 1960s, citing Vince Gironda's wide-grip variation, and that Jack LaLanne promoted dips on television.[1] These claims come from a single non-human-edited source.

Direct research on dips is limited. Grokipedia describes electromyographic work ranking dips highly for triceps activation, with recruitment of the triceps heads near that of a reference push-up variant.[1] A systematic review and meta-analysis of low-load versus high-load resistance training reports hypertrophy and strength adaptations across loading ranges, which applies to any progressively loaded exercise.[3]

Deep dips place the shoulder in extension under body weight. Sources describe improper form as potentially causing anterior shoulder impingement and increased shear forces at the joint, and say the exercise may need modification for people with existing shoulder or elbow problems.[1] Elbow tendon strain is also commonly reported anecdotally. Unstable stands are a separate equipment hazard.

Dips are discussed as a low-cost way to add pressing volume at home, often paired with pull-ups for balanced upper-body training. T Nation members list weighted ring dips among exercises for delts and traps, and mention dips alongside cables and machines as chest accessories to barbell and dumbbell pressing.[7][8] In a thread on slow calisthenics progress, a member points to another poster who made large gains over about two years.[9]
No studies found of dip bars or dips for appearance outcomes. Research on resistance training in general, including a meta-analysis of low- versus high-load training, exists.[3]

timeline.event: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn is credited in one source with developing the parallel bars within the Turnen gymnastics system.[1]
Dips are reported to become a core bodybuilding exercise, with Jack LaLanne promoting them on television.[1]
